extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers/students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or composing poetry (and poetic prose), with specific emphases on diction, imagination, truth to nature, originality of thought, and the educative habits that produce verbal precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict accuracy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Habituate ourselves to a strict accuracy of expression; the moral and intellectual importance of verbal precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses forming a sensitive taste by close acquaintance with masterpieces; accurate expression feeds the understanding and acts as an antidote in an age of corrupt eloquence. Education from boyhood in investigating the meaning, choice and position of every word fosters logical habit and mental accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untranslatableness as test of blameless style
rubrics_metrics.description: The infallible test of a blameless style: its untranslatableness in words of the same language without injury to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge explains 'meaning' includes not only the correspondent object but all associations a word recalls. Thus ideal diction resists easy paraphrase without loss of nuance; this is presented as the ultimate standard of purity and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning includes associations (language conveys attitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include in the meaning of a word not only its correspondent object, but likewise all the associations which it recalls; language conveys object, character, mood and intentions of the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating diction, judge whether words carry their associative freight (mood, character, intention) appropriately. Loss of associations through lax word-choice weakens poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectations and misappropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction should be preserved uncorrupted by the affectations and misappropriations which promiscuous authorship and disproportionate reading of contemporary compositions have rendered general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include fashionable, 'vicious' phraseology found across sermons, newspapers, political harangues, and social toasts; these infect writers who do not guard diction. The remedy is selective reading and deliberate choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of preserving pure style in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In prose it may be impossible to preserve style wholly unalloyed by vicious phraseology, because daily examples of tastelessness are so numerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare prose to poetry: while poetry can deliberate over every line, prose is more exposed to contagion. Education and early training in word-meaning mitigate this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education by investigating words builds judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A youth led from his first boyhood to investigate the meaning of every word and the reason of its choice and position will find logic presenting itself under new names and will cultivate judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is prescriptive: deliberately teach the young to think well by the same unremembered process by which they learn to speak; linguistic training produces habits that guard against fanaticism and indistinct watch-words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity to the intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is not necessarily obscure because it does not aim to be popular; it is enough if a work be perspicuous to those for whom it is written, and 'Fit audience find, though few.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscurity is tolerable when the poem's intended readers (e.g., contemplative or philosophic readers) can understand it. Coleridge cites Dante's lines to justify poems aimed at a smaller, accustomed readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and sanity of thoughts and sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent weight and sanity of the Thoughts and Sentiments, won not from books but from the poet’s own meditative observation; thoughts are fresh and original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poet’s reflections spring from personal meditative observation rather than borrowed lore. Freshness is shown even in small poems by 'just and original reflection' (several quoted passages provided as examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinewy strength and originality of lines and paragraphs (curiosa felicitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sinewy strength and originality of single lines and paragraphs; the frequent curiosa felicitas of his diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge emphasizes felicitous, strikingly original phrasing (single lines/paragraphs) as a hallmark of excellence; critics acknowledge and admire such diction even when they attack the poet on other grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect truth of nature in images and descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect truth of nature in images and descriptions as taken immediately from nature, showing a long and genial intimacy with the spirit that gives physiognomic expression to nature’s works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images should reflect nature with softness and lustre rather than distortion; genius brings out veins and tints overlooked by common observation. Coleridge gives numerous examples (skating, green linnet, blue-cap, cuckoo, 'Three years she grew...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditative pathos and contemplative sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: A meditative pathos: union of deep and subtle thought with sensibility; a sympathy with man as man, more of a contemplator than a fellow-sufferer, yet seeing the sameness of human nature beneath rank or misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet’s power to elicit heartfelt feeling through contemplative insight (examples: 'The Affliction of Margaret', 'The Mad Mother'). The poet should render human nature legible even under calamity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift of Imagination in the highest sense (not mere fancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gift of Imagination in the highest and strictest sense: an imaginative power that consecrates and adds 'the light that never was'—not mere or unmodified fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative power should be original and profound (Coleridge likens Wordsworth’s imagination to Shakespeare and Milton in kind, though distinct). Excessive strangeness or forced likeness is a potential defect: imagination should feel spontaneous and appropriate (examples: Yew Trees, Resolution and Independence, sonnets, 'Ode on the Intimations...').
